_**Agent (gpt-5.6-sol 2026-07-29 14:19:10Z)**_

The short answer: DeadReckon has built much of the hard execution kernel, but it has not yet delivered the complete original experience.

Today it is a serious local verified-run system. It is not yet a dependable “start this goal, walk away, and trust it to keep working until the goal is genuinely complete” product.

## Where the project stands

| Original promise | Current state | Assessment |
|---|---|---|
| Define “done” before starting | Plain English can be compiled into `acceptance.yaml`; an LLM critic looks for weak checks and goals a stub could satisfy | Strong, although users can still fall back to detected project tests instead of consciously approving a real contract |
| Run coding CLIs in isolation | Git worktree and copy isolation are mature; changes require deliberate promotion | Strong for source isolation |
| Keep running until the goal is met | A normal run is foreground and limited to 12 turns; recovery normally requires `resume`. Chain has detached execution; current uncommitted plan work adds orphan adoption | Major remaining gap |
| Independently judge completion | A separate gate runs deterministic checks and validates the completion marker | Strong deterministic floor, but not the semantic meta-judge described in the original vision |
| Resist a dishonest worker | The worker cannot bypass a failing test merely by claiming completion; tamper checks catch several forms of weakening | Useful protection, but current “cannot forge” language overstates the boundary |
| Capture the whole run | State, snapshots, events, traces, spend, provenance, implementation notes and reports are persisted | One of the strongest parts of the system |
| Make the experience pleasant | The default five-command interface is quite good | Internally, too many execution models and advanced commands still leak into the mental model |

The most important correction is about the judge. The LLM currently helps write and critique the definition of done in [acceptance.rs](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon/src/commands/acceptance.rs:642). Final acceptance is then deterministic. There is no independent LLM reading the original goal, the resulting change and the evidence and deciding whether the goal was semantically achieved.

That means the original `/goal` idea is only partly present: semantic judgment happens before execution, not at the final boundary.

The current run loop also has a real ceiling: normal runs configure 12 turns in [run.rs](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon/src/commands/run.rs:496), after which the loop fails with a budget-exhausted state. State is durable, but the worker is not automatically durable. If its supervising process disappears, the job waits for an operator to resume or adopt it.

## What has genuinely been achieved

DeadReckon now has a credible “verified run” primitive:

1. Create an isolated workspace.
2. establish a completion contract;
3. run a chosen coding CLI;
4. retain state and evidence after every turn;
5. respond to gate failures with another corrective turn;
6. accept only after the external gate passes;
7. deliberately promote or export the result.

That is substantial. The current working tree passed the complete workspace test suite: 2,049 tests passed and none failed. I did not modify the repository.

The evidence system is also unusually thorough. [RunView](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-core/src/run_view.rs:20) gives a useful read model over persisted state and ledgers. The promotion boundary in [promotion.rs](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-core/src/promotion.rs:25) makes “completed” meaningfully different from “applied to my repository.”

So this is not a speculative pile of commands. It contains a real, tested kernel.

## Necessary complexity

These are inherent to the product and should remain:

- Safely isolating and later promoting source changes.
- Supporting different CLI providers and their different streaming, cancellation and accounting behaviour.
- Durable job identity, state, locking, recovery and cancellation.
- Compiling acceptance criteria into executable checks.
- A semantic judge for requirements that cannot be reduced to tests.
- Preventing the worker from modifying its own acceptance mechanism.
- Recording enough evidence to explain why a result was accepted.
- Scheduling dependent and parallel units of verified work.
- Explicit budgets, deadlines and blocked states. “Until done” must not mean “loop forever.”

## Incidental complexity

This is complexity created by the current shape of the implementation rather than the underlying problem:

- Forty-five top-level command variants, even though most are hidden from ordinary help.
- Several overlapping journey concepts: run, chain, plan/fork/merge, campaign, reshape and others.
- Control truth spread across state JSON, several JSONL ledgers and sidecar files, requiring hand-written reconciliation and orphan adoption.
- Repeated provider, retry, narration and budget policies in different orchestration layers.
- Multiple documentation and narration pipelines.
- Compatibility aliases, no-op flags and old spellings.
- Making implementation-note production part of the completion ritual, rather than deriving the after-state account from captured evidence.
- Continuing to deepen campaigns, learning, narration and other secondary systems before unattended goal execution is fully dependable.

The architectural smell is: there is one good verified-run atom, but too many ways to arrange and supervise it.

## The trust-boundary problem

The README’s “it can’t fake the finish” claim is stronger than the current implementation warrants.

The gate nonce is stored inside the run directory, and the marker uses Rust’s `DefaultHasher` in [gate.rs](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-core/src/gate.rs:752), rather than a cryptographic MAC or signature. General CLI-provider and Bash-tool execution do not consistently deny access to gate material. In addition, automatic sandbox selection can fall back to no sandbox.

The system can truthfully say:

> A separate process runs the acceptance checks, and an existing completion marker cannot make failing checks pass.

It cannot yet universally say:

> A hostile coding agent is technically unable to forge acceptance.

Results should distinguish:

- `VERIFIED + CONFINED`
- `VERIFIED + UNCONFINED`
- `NEEDS REVIEW`
- `FAILED`

That would make the confidence claim precise rather than absolute.

## Where I would take it next

### 1. Finish the durable goal executor

Make `deadreckon start` create a durable local job, return its ID and detach by default. A small supervisor or user service should:

- lease pending jobs;
- recover abandoned leases;
- restart after terminal or machine failure;
- retain bounded retry, spend and time policies;
- distinguish blocked, cancelled, budget-exhausted and failed;
- supervise runs, chains and plans through the same scheduler.

Temporal is the useful exemplar here. Its core model is a durable execution reconstructed from an append-only event history, with explicit lifecycle operations such as start, describe, result, cancel, terminate and reset. DeadReckon should extract those durability and operator-semantics patterns without becoming a distributed workflow platform. [Temporal workflow execution](https://docs.temporal.io/workflow-execution), [Temporal CLI workflow commands](https://docs.temporal.io/cli/command-reference/workflow).

### 2. Restore the semantic meta-judge as a second key

Completion should require:

1. Deterministic checks pass.
2. An independent, read-only semantic judge assesses the goal, contract, diff and evidence.

The semantic judge must never override failed deterministic checks. It should return `achieved`, `revise` or `uncertain`, with evidence-backed reasons. If it is unavailable in strict mode, the result becomes `NEEDS REVIEW`, not accepted.

This is necessary complexity: natural-language goals cannot always be completely compiled into tests.

### 3. Close the gate boundary

- Keep signing material outside the agent-visible workspace.
- Use HMAC-SHA-256 or a proper signature.
- Deny gate and proof paths across every provider and tool route.
- Bind the receipt to the contract, policy, source revision and resulting revision.
- Fail closed for unattended trusted runs.
- Add adversarial tests in which an agent deliberately searches for and attempts to forge the marker.

### 4. Collapse the product around one job model

Keep the ordinary surface:

```text
start
attach
status
list
finish
```

Plans, chains and campaigns should become internal scheduling shapes or an explicitly advanced namespace. They should all create the same durable jobs and verified-run receipts.

Similarly, create one append-only control event history and derive current state and `RunView` from it. Rich spend, trace and documentation evidence can remain separate, but lifecycle truth should have one source.

### 5. Freeze secondary expansion and dogfood the promise

Temporarily freeze deeper campaign features, learning/improve surfaces and additional narration variants. Test the core promise on 20–30 real tasks across multiple repositories and providers.

Measure:

- unattended verified completion rate;
- automatic recovery rate;
- false acceptance and false rejection;
- number of operator interventions;
- time required to understand the final result;
- supervision and judging cost.

Kill the terminal, worker and machine during these trials. Remove network access. Attempt to tamper with the gate. Run DeadReckon on DeadReckon itself.

## Bottom line

DeadReckon contains a strong, unusually well-tested verified-run kernel inside an overgrown product.

The next phase should not be more orchestration features. It should make one promise completely true:

> Give DeadReckon a goal and an approved definition of done. It will work in isolation, survive interruptions, stop for explicit bounded reasons, independently verify both the checks and the meaning of the result, and leave behind a clear receipt explaining what happened.

Once that experience is reliable and pleasant, the plans, chains and campaigns become valuable multipliers instead of competing product models.

_**Agent (gpt-5.6-sol 2026-07-29 14:19:10Z)**_

“Finish the durable goal executor” means making DeadReckon responsible for the job after the user starts it.

Right now, DeadReckon has durable records, but not fully durable execution.

## Today

A normal run behaves roughly like this:

```text
Your terminal
    ↓
deadreckon run
    ↓
coding CLI
    ↓
gate
```

The `deadreckon run` process is the supervisor. While that process is alive, it keeps giving the coding CLI turns and checking the result.

DeadReckon saves enough state to recover, but:

- closing the supervisor stops the work;
- restarting the computer stops the work;
- someone must run `resume`;
- a normal attempt stops after 12 turns;
- detached execution exists for chains, but is not the common execution model.

That is resumable execution: “we can pick up where we stopped.”

It is not yet durable execution: “DeadReckon continues to own the job until it reaches a legitimate stopping point.”

## The proposed experience

The user should be able to do this:

```bash
deadreckon start "Add password reset"
```

DeadReckon would:

1. Create the isolated workspace.
2. Prepare and approve the definition of done.
3. Record a durable job.
4. Return a run ID immediately.
5. Let a background supervisor carry on.

```text
Started run dr-4821
Workspace: isolated
Status: running
Attach: deadreckon attach dr-4821
```

The terminal is no longer responsible for keeping the work alive.

```text
Terminal                 DeadReckon supervisor
   │                              │
   ├── start goal ───────────────→│
   │←── run ID ───────────────────┤
   │                              ├── run coding CLI
   │                              ├── save evidence
   │                              ├── run gate
   │                              ├── retry if appropriate
   │                              └── finish or stop explicitly
   │
   └── may close safely
```

`attach` would only observe or interact with the job. Disconnecting would not stop it.

## What keeps it durable

The background supervisor needs four basic mechanisms.

### A durable queue

`start` writes the goal into a local queue before execution begins:

```text
Job: dr-4821
Goal: Add password reset
Contract: acceptance.yaml
State: queued
Budget: $20
Deadline: 4 hours
Workspace: /path/to/worktree
```

If no supervisor is currently running, DeadReckon starts one.

### Leases and heartbeats

When a supervisor takes a job, it records:

```text
dr-4821 is leased by process 9312 until 14:35:00
```

It renews that lease periodically.

If the process crashes, the lease expires. Another supervisor can safely adopt the job. This prevents both abandonment and two supervisors working the same job simultaneously.

The uncommitted plan changes currently in the repository are moving towards this kind of orphan adoption, but it should become a shared facility for every execution shape.

### Checkpoints after every important event

DeadReckon already persists much of this. The durable executor would formalize events such as:

```text
Job started
Turn 1 started
Turn 1 completed
Gate failed
Corrective turn requested
Turn 2 completed
Gate passed
Semantic judge passed
Run verified
```

After a crash, the replacement supervisor reads this history and knows what to do next. It does not start the entire job again.

### Explicit stopping reasons

“Keep running until done” should not mean infinite retries.

A job may stop because it is:

```text
VERIFIED
BLOCKED — requires user decision
BUDGET_EXHAUSTED
DEADLINE_REACHED
FAILED — unrecoverable error
CANCELLED
```

Those states are part of the confidence model. Quietly dying because a terminal closed is not.

## It does not require a large distributed system

This could initially be a small local service:

```text
deadreckond
```

On macOS it could run through `launchd`; Linux could use a user-level `systemd` service. DeadReckon could also begin with a simpler detached conductor process, provided it has leases and automatic adoption.

It does not need Kubernetes, a server database or a cloud account. SQLite or an append-only local event log would be sufficient.

## Why this is the highest-priority gap

The original promise is not primarily “we save excellent records.” It is:

> Give the system a goal and trust it to carry responsibility for reaching a verified conclusion.

Without a durable executor, the human still carries part of that responsibility:

- keeping the process alive;
- noticing that it stopped;
- deciding whether to resume;
- restarting orchestration after a crash.

With it, the human only intervenes when DeadReckon produces an intentional `BLOCKED` state.

A practical definition of done for this feature would include:

- Start a run and close the terminal: it continues.
- Kill the coding CLI: DeadReckon retries or records a clear failure.
- Kill the supervisor: another supervisor adopts the run.
- Restart the computer: unfinished jobs resume automatically.
- Never run the same turn twice concurrently.
- Respect spend, time and retry limits.
- Preserve the same run ID, workspace and evidence throughout.
- Finish only through the normal verification boundary.

That change would turn DeadReckon from a well-persisted foreground runner into the “start it and trust it” product described in the original goal.

+pub fn gate_key_path(paths: &DeadreckonPaths, run_id: &str) -> PathBuf {

+
+pub fn gate_key_path_for_run_root(run_root: &Path, run_id: &str) -> Result<PathBuf> {
+    let home = run_root
+        .parent()
+        .and_then(Path::parent)
+        .and_then(Path::parent)
+        .and_then(Path::parent)
+        .ok_or_else(|| {
+            DeadreckonError::InvalidInput(format!(
+                "cannot infer DeadReckon home from run root {}",
+                run_root.display()
+            ))
+        })?;
+    Ok(gate_key_path(
+        &DeadreckonPaths::from_home(home),
+        run_id,
+    ))
+}
+
+pub fn create_gate_key(paths: &DeadreckonPaths, run_id: &str) -> Result<Vec<u8>> {
+    let first = Uuid::new_v4();
+    let second = Uuid::new_v4();
+    let mut key = Vec::with_capacity(GATE_KEY_BYTES);
+    key.extend_from_slice(first.as_bytes());
+    key.extend_from_slice(second.as_bytes());
+    write_gate_key(paths, run_id, &key)?;
+    Ok(key)
+}
+
+pub fn write_gate_key(paths: &DeadreckonPaths, run_id: &str, key: &[u8]) -> Result<()> {
+    if key.len() != GATE_KEY_BYTES {
+        return Err(DeadreckonError::InvalidInput(format!(
+            "gate key must be {GATE_KEY_BYTES} bytes, got {}",
+            key.len()
+        )));
+    }

+    let parent = path.parent().ok_or_else(|| {
+        DeadreckonError::InvalidInput(format!("gate key path {} has no parent", path.display()))
+    })?;
+    std::fs::create_dir_all(parent).with_path(parent)?;
+
+    let mut options = OpenOptions::new();
+    options.write(true).create_new(true);
+    #[cfg(unix)]
+    {
+        use std::os::unix::fs::OpenOptionsExt;
+        options.mode(0o600);

+fn hex_encode(bytes: &[u8]) -> String {
+    const HEX: &[u8; 16] = b"0123456789abcdef";
+    let mut output = String::with_capacity(bytes.len() * 2);
+    for byte in bytes {
+        output.push(char::from(HEX[usize::from(byte >> 4)]));
+        output.push(char::from(HEX[usize::from(byte & 0x0f)]));
+    }
+    output

+fn hex_decode(value: &str) -> std::result::Result<Vec<u8>, String> {

+    }
+    let mut output = Vec::with_capacity(value.len() / 2);
+    for pair in value.as_bytes().chunks_exact(2) {
+        let high = hex_nibble(pair[0])?;
+        let low = hex_nibble(pair[1])?;
+        output.push((high << 4) | low);
+    }
+    Ok(output)

+fn hex_nibble(value: u8) -> std::result::Result<u8, String> {

+        b'a'..=b'f' => Ok(value - b'a' + 10),
+        b'A'..=b'F' => Ok(value - b'A' + 10),
+        _ => Err("hex value contains a non-hex character".to_string()),

+            Some("true") => true,
+            Some("false") => false,
+            Some(value) => {

+                    "{GATE_CONTAINED_ENV} must be true or false, got {value}"
+                ));
+            }
+            None => return Err(format!("{GATE_CONTAINED_ENV} is required")),
+        };
+        let containment = if contained {
+            AcceptanceContainment::contained(backend)
+        } else {
+            AcceptanceContainment::uncontained(backend)
+        };
+        Ok(Self { key, containment })

+    command

 pub fn create_gate_key(paths: &DeadreckonPaths, run_id: &str) -> Result<Vec<u8>> {

+    // UUID v4 uses the platform CSPRNG but reserves version/variant bits. Hash
+    // three independent UUIDs so the stored 32-byte key has at least 256 bits
+    // of random input without adding a second OS-random dependency surface.

_**Agent (gpt-5.6-sol 2026-07-29 14:40:24Z)**_

Implemented Binnacle/Watchkeeper gate hardening P1–P4.

Key outcomes:

- New runs create `~/.deadreckon/gate-keys/<run-id>.key`, outside the run root, mode `0600`.
- Key filenames are escaped so crafted run IDs cannot traverse outside the key store.
- New markers use schema v2 with HMAC-SHA-256 and constant-time verification.
- Canonical bytes bind checks, tamper evidence, campaign roll-up, issuer, proof kind, containment and resolved sandbox backend.
- Missing v2 keys fail closed with a runnable `deadreckon verdict` hint.
- Existing v1 nonce markers still validate through the original algorithm and report `LegacyWeak`; they are never native gate proof.
- Synthetic controller markers are explicitly `SyntheticController`; `is_native_gate_proof()` rejects them.
- `dr-gate` receives key and containment only through environment inputs and never resolves the key path.
- Repository-controlled acceptance subprocesses explicitly remove all signing environment variables, preventing build/test scripts from leaking the key.
- Cleanup and abandon do not delete keys; key lifetime remains aligned with retained evidence.

Files changed:

- `Cargo.toml`
- `Cargo.lock`
- `DEPENDENCIES.md`
- `crates/deadreckon-core/Cargo.toml`
- `crates/deadreckon-core/src/gate.rs`
- `crates/deadreckon-core/src/state.rs`
- `crates/deadreckon-core/src/lib.rs`
- `crates/deadreckon/src/bin/dr-gate.rs`

Primary APIs added:

- `gate_key_path`, `create_gate_key`, `read_gate_key`, `write_gate_key`
- `encode_gate_key`, `decode_gate_key`
- `AcceptanceContainment`
- `AcceptanceProofKind`
- `AcceptanceSignatureStrength`
- `canonical_marker_bytes`
- `v2_marker_signature`, `verify_v2_marker_signature`
- `write_native_acceptance_marker_with_results_and_key`
- `AcceptanceMarker::is_native_gate_proof()`

Verification:

- `cargo test -p deadreckon-core`: 210 unit tests plus all core integration and doc tests passed.
- `cargo test -p deadreckon --bin dr-gate`: 2/2 passed.
- Gate-focused suite: 36/36 passed.
- `git diff --check`: passed.
- Core clippy reaches only one unrelated concurrent finding in `completion.rs:305` (`manual_is_multiple_of`); gate code has no reported clippy finding.

Intentionally remaining:

- P5–P7 denylist wiring, Seatbelt deny-by-default and hostile-backend tests.
- User-facing v1 weak/synthetic labels in `RunView`, verdict and reports remain P10 work.
- A `0600` same-UID key is not sufficient under sandbox `none`; those receipts must remain explicitly uncontained.
- Actual evidence-purge logic must eventually remove the retained key.
